title: Zenith Payments - Incident postmortem follow-up
summary: Follow-up after 2027-04-28 production incident: discussed root cause (autoscaler + batching/quant mismatch), mitigations deployed (rate-limits, fallback routing), short-term mitigations, and next steps for reliability improvements and a verification run. Agreed on timelines for bench tests, config guardrails, and a SOC2/audit doc share.
action_items: Priya Desai - run full end-to-end benchmark (1M tokens, peak concurrency pattern) against current Dedicated config and share results - due 2027-05-09
Liam O'Connor - provide exact traffic shape for 2027-04-28 incident (hourly time series + histogram of request lengths) - due 2027-05-06
Alex Murphy - share updated security pack (SOC2 scope, SSO docs, KMS integration notes) and incident timeline slide deck - due 2027-05-04
Mei Chen - confirm internal change freeze window and availability for verification run (target week of 2027-05-16) - due 2027-05-07
next_steps: Redwood to run bench and post results to shared folder + interpretation notes
Customer to grant a scoped read-only access to traffic telemetry and release windows
Schedule verification run the week of 2027-05-16
Agree on config guardrails to prevent autoscaler thrash and oversized batches
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-05-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48m
Recording: yes

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you making the time. Quick roll call - Alex here from Redwood, Priya is joining from our SRE/serving team.
[00:12] Mei (Zenith): Hi all, Mei here.
[00:15] Liam (Zenith): Liam on SRE.
[00:18] Rex (Zenith): Rex, CTO.
[00:20] Priya (Redwood SE): Hi, thanks. We'll pick up from the timeline you sent. The goal for today is to confirm the RCA we shared, walk through the mitigations we rolled out, and agree on the verification plan and owners.

[01:02] Alex: Quick recap for folks who didn't read the full deck - on 2027-04-28 at ~09:40 UTC you saw a spike in 99th latency and several model endpoints started failing with OOMs, which cascaded to the autoscaler and then to routing fallbacks not kicking in until later. That was the visible outage.

[01:28] Mei: Right. Our initial and slightly embarrasing note - we had a config drift where the Dedicated pool had a new kernel/quantization build that increased peak memory per shard, and the autoscaler was set to scale by node count but with a cooldown that was too long. So when the traffic hit, batches grew and KV cache pressure spiked.

[01:52] Priya: Yeah, and on top of that we saw a mismatch between the model's quant profile and the runtime kernel selection. The runtime picked a path that ended up using slightly more GPU memory than expected for long-context requests. There's also a mis-ordered fallback rule in the routing policy: fallback to a smaller model variant existed, but it was lower priority than cross-region fallback, so by the time it tried cross-region, capacity in the other region was saturated.

[02:24] Liam: We also noticed some transcription/telemetry gaps - a few requests didn't have full KV cache metrics, so correlating which requests were hitting the cold path was harder.

[03:00] Alex: That's a great point. We documented that in the RCA: root cause is multi-factor - (1) quant/kernel mismatch causing higher per-token memory, (2) autoscaler cooldown too long + scale granularity mis-set, (3) routing/fallback priority misconfiguration, and (4) insufficient telemetry for cold-path requests.

[03:35] Rex: Sounds right. Can you run through exactly what you pushed right after the incident? We want clarity on which mitigations were hotfixes vs. longer-term changes.

[03:50] Priya: Sure. Short term, within 2 hours we: applied emergency rate-limits to the busiest routes (per-key QPS cap), lowered the max batch size for long-context endpoints, tightened autoscaler cooldown to 30s for scale-up, and temporarily changed routing priority so model-variant fallback happens before cross-region. We also backrolled the newest kernel/quant build to the previous stable build.

[04:28] Mei: Did the K-V cache eviction policy change? I remember we saw a bunch of cache thrash.

[04:35] Priya: We adjusted the KV eviction threshold conservatively - for the hotfix we moved from a 70% utilization threshold to 55% to force earlier eviction and reduce spike pressure. That increased API token cost a bit during the following window but avoided OOMs.

[05:00] Liam: After the hotfixes latency looked better, but we still want an assurance this won't recur during black friday-like spike.

[05:12] Alex: Understood. So the medium-term plan we propose has three workstreams: improved telemetry + tag propagation so per-request cache/memory signals are available; config guardrails (autoscaler bounds, batch size caps based on request-length distribution); and better rollout/testing (pre-prod stress tests that replicate the traffic shape).

[05:45] Priya: For telemetry we're going to add a KV cache tag at request ingress and ensure it's passed through so you can see hit/miss ratios per route. We'll also include a per-request est_peak_mem metric that the runtime can emit. That should address the correlation gap Liam mentioned.

[06:10] Mei: How intrusive are these telemetry changes? We can't allow anything that adds significant p99 latency overhead.

[06:20] Priya: The telemetry is emitted asynchronously to the observability pipeline - we sample 100% for the verification window then switch to 10% after stability is proven. Latency overhead is <1ms on average in our staging tests.

[06:42] Rex: About the autoscaler - I want a hard guardrail. For example, don't scale below X GPUs during business hours, or don't allow batch sizes above Y for 90th percentile request length. Can you codify that?

[06:58] Alex: Yes, those are config guardrails. We can add per-route scalar min/max nodes and batch-size caps that are enforced by the control plane. We'll make those configurable via the console and also provide a JSON guardrail config you can check into your infra repo.

[07:24] Mei: Great. On rollouts: can we do canary at 5% with traffic shaping, and if memory usage trend rises > 15% in 10 minutes, auto-roll back?

[07:35] Priya: Absolutely. We have canary policies and auto-rollbacks. We'll set up the policy you described as part of the verification run.

[08:02] Liam: On the verification run - what's your plan for reproducing the traffic shape? We can't share prod secrets but we'll provide aggregates and a replay token.

[08:15] Priya: We'll run our stress harness in your staging environment with a replay of anonymized traffic shapes you share. We'll also run a synthetic mix that includes long-context tails to exercise the memory path. Expect multiple runs at increasing QPS. We'll capture memory, batch size distribution, KV hit rate, and token throughput.

[08:45] Mei: Timeline?

[08:48] Alex: We propose Redwood runs an initial bench by 2027-05-09 and then schedule a joint verification week of 2027-05-16. That gives you time to set a change freeze and provide telemetry slices.

[09:05] Rex: Sounds reasonable. A couple security items: we need the incident timeline and audit logs, and we want to confirm KMS/HSM integration for customer managed keys. Also SOC2 scope details.

[09:18] Alex: I'll send the security pack and an incident timeline slide deck. Regarding KMS, Redwood Private supports customer KMS/HSM; for Dedicated we can integrate your KMS for certain key classes - I'll include the integration notes. SOC2 material is included in the pack.

[09:38] Mei: On the topic of logs, can we get a proof that audit logs include per-request route and model version? We have compliance to show.

[09:50] Priya: Yes, audit logs include route, model version, and a request-id. We'll provide a sample masked log extract.

[10:05] Liam: One operational detail - during the incident the autoscaler cooldown prevented scale-up for ~7 min; is that from the default cluster autoscaler or Redwood's internal autoscaling layer?

[10:17] Priya: That was Redwood's internal autoscaler interacting badly with the cluster autoscaler. The misconfiguration was that policy cooldown was set too long and scale increment was small (1 GPU at a time) which was too slow for that spike. We tightened cooldown and also changed scale steps to be proportional to current load delta.

[10:40] Rex: Any residual risk after the hotfixes and planned work? Be blunt.

[10:46] Alex: Residual risk is moderate until verification passes. Possibilities: an extreme tail request mix could still drive memory above expectations if a new model build changes kernel behavior; also cross-region capacity constraints could still happen if both regions experience simultaneous spikes. The mitigation is guardrails, better fallback priority, and runbook-driven escalation.

[11:15] Mei: Ok, let's talk responsibilities. Who owns the verification harness run and interpretation?

[11:22] Priya: Redwood will own the harness runs; Zenith will provide traffic shape, staging endpoints, and a release window. We'll pair on interpretation.

[11:40] Alex: Recap of immediate deliverables: Redwood shares security pack + RCA slides (Alex) by 2027-05-04; Redwood bench results by 2027-05-09 (Priya); Zenith provides traffic histograms + change freeze confirmation by 2027-05-07 (Liam/Mei). Then joint verification week 2027-05-16.

[12:02] Liam: Quick question from the engineering team - can you add a pinned metric for per-model est_peak_mem so our dashboards can alert before OOM?

[12:12] Priya: Yes, we'll surface est_peak_mem and a derived alert when the 95th est_peak_mem crosses 80% of GPU mem. We'll share a Grafana dashboard template.

[12:36] Mei: Also want a postmortem note phrasing - we need a single page summary for execs. Can you produce that?

[12:44] Alex: We'll include a 1-page exec summary in the deck.

[13:00] Rex: Anything else?

[13:06] Mei: I want to call out cost - you mentioned the hotfix increased token cost because of lowered cache threshold; can we put in a cost offset for the next month?

[13:16] Alex: We're open to looking at that - we'll include a note on usage deltas in the postmortem and follow up via the AE channel on potential credits for the short-term increased cost.

[13:34] Priya: One more technical nit - the mismatch that caused the kernel selection is a build-time change in one of the runtime's heuristics for long sequences. We've already reverted the build, but longer-term we'll add a canary job that runs memory regressions on pre-merge.

[13:54] Liam: Good.

[14:00] Alex: Ok let's close with explicit next steps and owners - I'll type them up and post to the shared folder after this call. Thanks everyone.

[14:15] Mei: Thanks.
[14:18] Rex: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
